summary:
The department of Vaupés stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

Day-to-day conduct in Vaupés is regulated by a different layer of authority. The department operates under an orden público regime in which armed groups rather than the departmental police hold effective control, and a 2025 national LGBTIQ+ report documents the territorial expansion of violence against LGBTIQ+ people together with the insufficiency of the state response, noting that trans women are displaced from their regions by the same armed actors that displace other residents. No department-specific enforcement or incident data for Vaupés was located.

A trans visitor should therefore expect the formal protections of the national framework to depend in practice on actors who are not the police, and should read the documented armed-group targeting of trans women in other Colombian departments as the operative model of risk. Lethal anti-trans violence in the country has occurred in broad daylight, been filmed by bystanders, and ended without an arrest even after a presidential order to investigate.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern a visitor should generalise from is territorial and driven by armed groups rather than by ordinary crime. In Caquetá department, armed groups ran a "social cleansing" campaign in which flyers on the streets and circulated over WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men that she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, and then fled at night; a second trans woman reported that a friend of hers was killed. Trans women in that department reported few options beyond sex work, and discrimination confines trans women nationally mainly to hairdressing or sex work. In Guajira department, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Targeted killings also continue in ordinary urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín on 4 April 2025; the assault was filmed and the 28-second video went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands before she drowned in a creek. She died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents and President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, but no one had been arrested as of the report of 14 April 2025, and her mother Sandra Borja stated that she was killed for being who she was. Solidarity events were held in several cities.

The scale figures are national. One report counted 13 trans people killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025, another recorded eight trans women killed between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and the Attorney General's Office logged 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and lived experience are disconnected and that killings are rising.
localsOnly:
For Colombian residents, legal gender recognition requires no court order and no medical evidence: since June 2015 the marker is changed by signing a document before a notary, and the Constitutional Court has recognised self-recognition as the basis since 1993. The official Reyes, who defended the 2015 change, described the former examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Marriage equality dates from 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples from 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law remained before the legislature in 2025.

Courts and international mechanisms have also intervened on detention and on conflict-related violence. A Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against them constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no Vaupés-specific enforcement data, incident records or departmental violence statistics were located in the sources. The armed-group "social cleansing" campaigns, kill-list flyers and death threats documented for Caquetá and Guajira have not been reported for Vaupés, and the sources do not establish whether comparable campaigns operate there.

Not sourced: which armed groups hold effective control in Vaupés, how the orden público regime is administered in the department, and whether notary-based marker changes are practically accessible to residents of Vaupés are all absent from the inventory. Whether the 2025 national LGBTIQ+ report contains Vaupés-level figures is also unresolved, as are the specific cities visited by Graeme Reid in May 2025.

The dating of individual incidents is taken at face value from the reports: Sara Millerey was attacked on 4 April 2025 with the video circulating from 5 April and her death recorded that afternoon, while the Guardian's Caquetá account was published on 30 July 2024. Whether arrests followed in any of these cases beyond what is stated is not resolved.
